title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #186: Non-Averaging Sets**

What is the maximum size of a non-averaging subset of {1,...,N}?

**Answer:** F(N) = N^(1/4+o(1))

The problem was originally due to Straus and resolved through work spanning 35 years:
- Lower bound: Bosznay (1989) via number-theoretic construction
- Upper bound: Pham-Zakharov (2024), improving Conlon-Fox-Pham (2023)
- Earlier upper bound: Erdős-Sárközy (1990)
mathContext: A set is non-averaging if no element equals the mean of two other distinct elements. This is weaker than avoiding all 3-term arithmetic progressions.
prerequisites: the arithmetic mean of two elements

title: Non-Averaging Set Definition
content:
**IsNonAveraging:**

A set A is non-averaging if no element is the arithmetic mean of two distinct other elements.

**Definition:**
```lean
def IsNonAveraging (A : Finset N) : Prop :=
  forall a in A, forall b in A, forall c in A,
    b != a -> c != a -> b != c -> 2 * a != b + c
```

Equivalently: no centered 3-term arithmetic progressions. The condition 2a != b + c prevents a from being the midpoint of b and c.
mathContext: This is a weaker condition than AP-freeness. AP-free sets avoid all 3-term APs, while non-averaging sets only avoid those centered at an element of the set.

title: Alternative Formulation
content:
**IsNonAveraging':**

Alternative definition using ordered triples: for a < b < c in A, the common difference b - a must differ from c - b.

This is equivalent to IsNonAveraging but sometimes easier to work with when elements are ordered.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of alternative formulation

title: Maximum Non-Averaging Set Size
content:
**F(N):**

The maximum size of a non-averaging subset of {1,...,N}.

Defined as the supremum of cardinalities over all non-averaging subsets of the range {0,...,N}. This is the central quantity in the problem.
mathContext: F(N) is a monotone non-decreasing function of N. Understanding its growth rate is the core question.

title: Empty Set is Non-Averaging
content:
**empty_is_nonAveraging:**

The empty set is trivially non-averaging — there are no elements to average.

Proved by contradiction: assuming a is in the empty set leads immediately to a contradiction via Finset.not_mem_empty.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of empty set is non-averaging

title: Singletons are Non-Averaging
content:
**singleton_is_nonAveraging:**

Any set with one element is non-averaging.

With only one element, the conditions b != a and c != a cannot both be satisfied since b and c must also be in the singleton {n}.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of singletons are non-averaging
prerequisites: the need for three distinct elements

title: Pairs are Non-Averaging
content:
**pair_is_nonAveraging:**

Any set with two distinct elements is non-averaging.

**Proof:** With only two elements a and b, we need three distinct elements x, y, z in the set, but can only pick from {a, b}. By pigeonhole, at least two must be equal, contradicting the distinctness requirements.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of pairs are non-averaging
prerequisites: the need for three distinct elements

title: Bosznay's Lower Bound (1989)
content:
**bosznay_lower_bound:**

There exist non-averaging sets of size >= N^(1/4) / 2.

Bosznay's construction uses number-theoretic techniques — selecting elements based on representations as sums of two squares or similar combinatorial structures — to build large non-averaging subsets of {1,...,N}.

**Reference:** Bosznay, "On the lower estimation of non-averaging sets", Acta Math. Hungar. (1989).
mathContext: This achieves the correct exponent 1/4. The construction is explicit but the proof that it works requires careful analysis.
prerequisites: axioms as stated assumptions in the formalization

title: Lower Bound Corollary
content:
**lower_bound_quarter:**

F(N) >= (1/2) * N^(1/4) for all N >= 1.

This follows from Bosznay's construction: the witness set has cardinality at least N^(1/4)/2, and F(N) is the supremum over all non-averaging sets.

Axiomatized because extracting F(N) >= |A| from the supremum definition requires showing the Finset.sup dominates any member.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of lower bound corollary

title: Erdős-Sárközy Upper Bound (1990)
content:
**erdos_sarkozy_upper_bound_1990:**

Original upper bound: F(N) <= C * (N log N)^(1/2).

This was the first non-trivial upper bound, proved by Erdős and Sárközy in their 1990 paper "On a problem of Straus." The bound has exponent 1/2, far from the lower bound exponent of 1/4.
mathContext: The gap between exponents 1/4 and 1/2 persisted for over 30 years.
prerequisites: axioms as stated assumptions in the formalization

title: Conlon-Fox-Pham (2023)
content:
**conlon_fox_pham_upper_bound_2023:**

Improved upper bound: F(N) <= C * N^(1/4) * (log N)^c for some constants C, c > 0.

This major improvement brought the exponent down to 1/4 (matching the lower bound), with only a polylogarithmic factor remaining.

**Reference:** Conlon-Fox-Pham, "Homogeneous structures in subset sums and non-averaging sets" (2023).
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of conlon-fox-pham (2023)
prerequisites: axioms as stated assumptions in the formalization

title: Pham-Zakharov Sharp Bound (2024)
content:
**pham_zakharov_upper_bound_2024:**

Sharp upper bound: for any epsilon > 0, F(N) <= C * N^(1/4+epsilon) for all sufficiently large N.

This essentially resolves the problem by matching the lower bound up to sub-polynomial factors. The o(1) term in the exponent is necessary — the bound cannot be improved to exactly N^(1/4).

**Reference:** Pham-Zakharov, "A sharp upper bound for the Erdős-Straus non-averaging sets problem" (2024).
mathContext: The formulation with forall epsilon captures the N^(1/4+o(1)) asymptotic precisely.
prerequisites: axioms as stated assumptions in the formalization

title: Main Bounds Theorem
content:
**erdos_186_bounds:**

Combines the lower and upper bounds into a single statement:

(1/2) * N^(1/4) <= F(N) <= C * N^(1/4+epsilon)

for any epsilon > 0, with C depending on epsilon.

**Proof:** Uses the Bosznay lower bound axiom and Pham-Zakharov upper bound axiom directly. The constant c = 1/2 comes from the lower bound construction.
mathContext: This is the key result that establishes F(N) = N^(1/4+o(1)).

title: Erdős Problem #186: Asymptotic Form
content:
**erdos_186:**

The o(1) exponent form: for any epsilon > 0, eventually
N^(1/4-epsilon) <= F(N) <= N^(1/4+epsilon).

This is the standard asymptotic notation meaning the exponent converges to 1/4. Axiomatized because deriving the lower bound in the form N^(1/4-epsilon) from Bosznay's construction requires careful asymptotic analysis beyond the direct N^(1/4)/2 bound.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of erdős problem #186: asymptotic form

title: Hereditary Property
content:
**nonAveraging_subset:**

Subsets of non-averaging sets are non-averaging.

**Proof:** If A is non-averaging and B is a subset of A, any three distinct elements in B are also in A. Since A satisfies the non-averaging condition for all triples, so does B.

This makes the family of non-averaging sets a downward-closed (hereditary) family.
mathContext: Hereditary properties are fundamental in extremal set theory. They ensure that the extremal function F(N) is well-behaved.

title: No Centered Arithmetic Progressions
content:
**nonAveraging_no_centered_AP:**

In a non-averaging set, for any three distinct elements a, b, c, b cannot be the midpoint: 2b != a + c.

**Proof:** Direct application of IsNonAveraging with reordered arguments, using symmetry of the "not equal" conditions.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of no centered arithmetic progressions

title: Roth's Theorem Connection
content:
**roth_bound_comparison:**

F(N) >= C * N / log N for some constant C > 0.

This axiom captures the key comparison with Roth's theorem: sets avoiding ALL 3-term APs have size at most N / log N (Roth 1953). Since non-averaging is a weaker condition (only avoiding centered APs), non-averaging sets can be much larger. Indeed, F(N) ~ N^(1/4) >> N / log N.
mathContext: Roth's theorem is a cornerstone of additive combinatorics. The comparison shows non-averaging is fundamentally different from AP-freeness.
prerequisites: axioms as stated assumptions in the formalization
